title: Understanding /etc/skel/ in Linux
markdown:
# Understanding `/etc/skel/` in Linux

The `/etc/skel/` directory in Linux serves as a **template** for new user home directories. Whenever a new user is created, the contents of `/etc/skel/` are copied into their home directory (`/home/username`). This ensures that each new user starts with predefined settings and necessary configuration files.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/arch-diagram.svg)

In this lab, we will cover:
- The purpose of `/etc/skel/`
- How it works
- How to verify its functionality
- Customizing `/etc/skel/` for system-wide user configurations
- Practical examples

## What is `/etc/skel/`?

The `/etc/skel/` folder in Linux is like a **starter kit** for new users. `Skel` stands for `skeleton` because it provides the basic structure for a new user's home directory.  

Whenever a new user is created, the files and folders inside `/etc/skel/` are automatically copied to their home directory. This ensures that every user starts with essential configurations, default settings, and any necessary files. It’s a simple way to give new users a **consistent and ready-to-use setup** right from the start.

## **Purpose of `/etc/skel/`**

The primary function of `/etc/skel/` is to provide default configuration files for new users. This is useful for:
- Ensuring a **consistent user environment** across all new accounts.
- Providing **default shell configurations**, aliases, and environment variables.
- Setting up necessary directories or files required for user operations.

By default, `/etc/skel/` includes basic shell configuration files such as:
```bash
.bashrc   # User-specific bash settings
.profile  # Environment variables and login shell configuration
.bash_logout  # Commands executed when the user logs out
```
These files are copied to a new user's home directory automatically when an account is created.

## **How `/etc/skel/` Works**

When a new user is created using the `useradd` command with the `-m` flag, the system:
1. Creates a new home directory at `/home/username`.
2. Copies all files and directories from `/etc/skel/` into `/home/username/`.
3. Assigns ownership of the copied files to the new user.

## **Verifying `/etc/skel/` Functionality**

We can verify the functionality of `/etc/skel/` by:
1. Listing the files in `/etc/skel/`
2. Creating a new user and checking their home directory

###  List Files in `/etc/skel/`

We can list the files in `/etc/skel/` using the `ls` command.

```bash
ls -la /etc/skel/
```

This command lists all files including hidden files(files starting with `.`) in `/etc/skel/` with their permissions, ownership, and size.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image.png)

### **Example: Creating a New User**

Run the following command to create a new user:
```bash
sudo useradd -m testuser
```
Now, check the home directory of the new user:
```bash
ls -la /home/testuser/
```

You will see files from `/etc/skel/` copied over.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-1.png)

## **Customizing `/etc/skel/`**

You can modify `/etc/skel/` to include additional files or folders that every new user should have.

### **Example 1: Adding a Welcome Message**

To ensure every new user gets a welcome message, create a `welcome.txt` file:

```bash
echo "Welcome to this system, enjoy your stay!" | sudo tee /etc/skel/welcome.txt
```
Now, when a new user is created, they will have `welcome.txt` in their home directory.

Now, create a new user and check their home directory:

```bash
sudo useradd -m testuser2
ls -la /home/testuser2/
```

You will see `welcome.txt` in their home directory.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-2.png)

### **Example 2: Setting Up a Custom `.bashrc`**

If you want every new user to have custom shell aliases or environment variables, edit the `/etc/skel/.bashrc` file:

```bash
sudo vim /etc/skel/.bashrc
```

Add custom aliases and a welcome message at the end of the file:

```bash
# Custom aliases
alias myinfo='echo "Current user: $(whoami)"'
alias diskspace='df -h /'

# Welcome message displayed at login
echo "Welcome to your Linux environment!"
```

Save and exit. Every new user will now get this configuration in their `.bashrc`.

Now, create a new user to see if they inherit the modified `.bashrc`:

```bash
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash testuser3
```

Here, `-s /bin/bash` ensures that the new user will use the bash shell.

> **Note:** It's important to specify `/bin/bash` as the shell when creating the user, as some systems default to `/bin/sh` which doesn't process aliases in the same way as bash.

Switch to the new user using:

```bash
su - testuser3
```

When you switch to the user, you'll see output similar to this:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-3.png)

The SSH agent errors can be safely ignored - they're related to the container environment. The important part is that the welcome message appears at the end, confirming that your `.bashrc` modifications are working.

> **Note:** To solve the SSH agent errors, ensure all new user accounts have properly configured `.ssh` directories by including them in the `/etc/skel/` template with appropriate permissions.

Check If `.bashrc` Exists in the New User’s Home Directory:

```bash
ls -la /home/testuser3/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-4.png)

Check if the custom aliases are working:

```bash
myinfo
diskspace
```

You should see that the `myinfo` command displays the current username, and `diskspace` shows available disk space. You should also see the welcome message when opening a new shell session.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-5.png)

## **Example Scenarios**

### **Scenario 1: Preventing Certain Files from Being Copied**

If you do **not** want certain files from `/etc/skel/` to be copied to new users, you can remove them:

```bash
sudo rm /etc/skel/welcome.txt
```

This ensures new users won’t have this file.

Now, create a new user and check their home directory:

```bash
sudo useradd -m testuser4
ls -la /home/testuser4/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-6.png)

We can see that the `welcome.txt` file is not copied to the new user's home directory which was there in the previous user.

### **Scenario 2: Copying Files Manually After User Creation**

If a user was created without the `-m` flag and their home directory wasn’t automatically set up, you can manually copy files from `/etc/skel/`:

1. Create a new user without home directory:

    ```bash
    sudo useradd testuser5
    ```

2. Create a home directory for the new user:

    ```bash
    sudo mkdir /home/testuser5
    ```

3. Check if the new user's home directory has the files from `/etc/skel/`:

    ```bash
    ls -la /home/testuser5/
    ```

    There is no files from `/etc/skel/` in the new user's home directory. So, we need to copy them manually.

    ![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-7.png)

4. Copy files from `/etc/skel/` to the new user's home directory:

    ```bash
    sudo cp -r /etc/skel/. /home/testuser5/
    sudo chown -R testuser5:testuser5 /home/testuser5/
    ```

5. Check if the files from `/etc/skel/` are copied to the new user's home directory:

    ```bash
    ls -la /home/testuser5/
    ```

    You will see the files from `/etc/skel/` in the new user's home directory.

    ![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2005/images/image-8.png)

This ensures they receive the default configurations.

## **Conclusion**

The `/etc/skel/` directory is a **powerful tool** for setting up new user environments automatically. By customizing `/etc/skel/`, administrators can ensure a **consistent**, **pre-configured**, and **ready-to-use** environment for every new user.  

By leveraging `/etc/skel/`, you can automate user setups and maintain consistency across a multi-user Linux system.
